transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a missile fired at its airport in Riyadh yesterday.
A separate attack sparked a fire in a passenger terminal.
NPR's Eba Trawi says attacks on the airport by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels a day earlier
left more than a dozen people dead and hundreds injured.
Saudi Arabia had already suspended flights and operations at Riyadh airport
when an unknown projectile hit one of its passenger terminals for the second day in a row.
Yemen's Houthis have struck Saudi airports four times over the past week,
but Saturday's attacks are the deadliest on the capital, Riyadh, in more than a decade.
Among those killed was a U.S. citizen.
The Iran-backed group says its attacks are in response to more than 2,000 Saudi airstrikes
on Houthi areas in various parts of Yemen in recent weeks.
The group also says it hit an Aramco gas facility
and an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia's eastern province in the past 24 hours.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on those attacks.
Eba Trawi, NPR News, Dubai.
A federal judge is ordering the Trump administration
to temporarily stop airing its taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Trump.
They've been airing in recent weeks ahead of the November midterm elections.
NPR's Luke Garrett says U.S. District Court Judge Jennifer Rochon
is banning the ads for two weeks while a court case continues.
Judge Rochon ordered the Trump administration to pull its multimillion-dollar ad buy,
no later than Sunday night.
The ruling came after a coalition, including the nonprofit Common Cause,
challenged the taxpayer-funded Trump ads in New York federal court, arguing,
it violated congressional appropriation and government propaganda rules.
The White House had set aside $20 million for the taxpayer-funded Trump ads
court records show.
The campaign-styled ads began airing in September, sparking bipartisan concern.
Trump himself acknowledged the backlash in early October,
saying he'd pay for the ads himself.
Despite this, the commercials, which feature Trump and his political agenda,
continued to air nationwide.
The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the judge's order.
Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.
Thank God these are just material possessions that insurance will cover,
and me and my dog are okay, but man, oh man, this is pretty tough.
More than 20,000 homes and businesses are without power in Alabama this morning.
While street futures are higher, Dow futures are up 63 points.
This is NPR News.
Several senators, Republicans and Democrats are calling on President Trump
to scrap a deal with Moscow to import millions of tons of Russian diesel fuel.
Trump announced the agreement late last week in an effort to help lower diesel prices in the U.S.
Trump announced the move on social media, saying he struck the deal in a phone call
with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The senators, voicing their objections, say Trump did not consult Congress
before making the deal with Putin and questioned whether it's legal.
Some faith leaders are denouncing plans by the Pentagon to livestream December's execution
of the former U.S. Army major, who shot and killed more than a dozen people at Fort Hood, Texas.
Many more were injured in the 2009 attack.
NPR's Jason Derose reports.
The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops says the public execution
represents the "barbaric promotion of a death culture."
In a statement, Archbishop of Oklahoma City Paul Coakley says the act
would only further undermine the nation's moral fabric.
Nadell Hassan killed 13 people and injured dozens of others in 2009.
Episcopal Church Presiding Bishop Sean Roe calls the plan to livestream
the firing squad execution "reprehensible in the extreme."
He goes on to say the act would cause "moral injury" to everyone involved.
Many religious groups — Catholic, Protestant, Jewish, and Muslim — officially oppose the death penalty.
Jason Derose, NPR News.

topics.text: Saudi Arabia intercepts missile at Riyadh airport after Houthi attacks kill more than a dozen
Federal judge temporarily halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads promoting the president
Power outages leave more than 20,000 homes and businesses dark in Alabama
Senators from both parties urge Trump to scrap Russian diesel fuel import deal with Putin
Faith leaders denounce Pentagon plan to livestream December execution of Nidal Hasan
